analysis.one_liner: Gives individuals legal rights over their personal data and creates a federal agency to enforce online privacy rules.
analysis.headline: The Online Privacy Act of 2026, which would let people delete, correct, and control how companies use their personal data, was introduced in March 2026 with zero cosponsors and referred to three House committees, where it awaits action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Digital Privacy Agency to enforce new rules on companies that collect personal information online. People would get rights to see what data companies hold about them, correct or delete it, take their data to competitors, and demand human review of automated decisions about jobs, credit, or housing. Companies would need explicit consent to sell personal data or use it for targeted ads, could not use manipulative designs to trick people into agreeing, and would face new security and breach-notification duties. The bill also makes it a federal crime to post someone's personal information with intent to threaten or harass them.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, ordinary internet users would gain enforceable rights over their personal data: the right to see what companies hold about them, correct or delete it, move it to a competitor, and get human review of automated decisions that affect jobs, credit, insurance, housing, or health care. Consumers would also gain stronger defaults against secret data collection for ad profiling, plus a private right of action and whistleblower protections. Small businesses are carved out of most duties, so the burden falls on large data companies rather than independent sellers.

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals rights to access, correct, delete, and port their data, and to get human review of consequential automated decisions about things like jobs, credit, insurance, housing, and health care.
Requires companies to collect and keep only the minimum data needed, get affirmative consent before behavioral profiling, and obtain consent before selling or disclosing data to third parties.

Bans manipulative 'dark patterns' in consent screens and prohibits processing that discriminates on the basis of race, sex, disability, and other protected classes, including a disparate-impact standard.

Creates a dedicated Digital Privacy Agency to investigate and litigate violations, with backstop enforcement by state attorneys general, private lawsuits, and whistleblower provisions, and bans forced arbitration of privacy claims.
Adds a federal crime, punishable by up to 5 years, for disclosing someone's personal information with intent to threaten, intimidate, or harass them ('doxxing').

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from collecting and selling personal data — ad-tech firms, data brokers, and large internet platforms — would bear compliance costs, restrictions on behavioral profiling and targeted advertising, and enforcement risk from the new agency, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ad-tech firms, data brokers, big platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose substantial compliance costs on virtually every online business: it covers any company that collects and shares personal information online, exempting only small businesses under tight thresholds (fewer than 200 employees, under $25 million in revenue, and little ad-based income), and some of those costs would likely be passed to consumers as poorer or paywalled services.
It bans companies from enforcing pre-dispute arbitration agreements for claims under the Act, which businesses argue pushes disputes into court rather than faster arbitration.

The bill concentrates broad rulemaking power in a single new Digital Privacy Agency Director, whose rules on things like advertising identifiers and discrimination standards would govern the entire internet economy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give ordinary people meaningful control over their personal data at a real cost to companies whose business models depend on harvesting it — a cost that would partly show up as less free, more heavily personalized online services and higher compliance burdens for small businesses. The main design concerns are that it is sweeping (it covers virtually every website and app, not just data brokers or big platforms), that it relies on a new agency to write most of the operative rules, and that its arbitration ban limits consumers' choice of forum. Its prospects of passage look remote, so the more practical cost so far is opportunity: no federal privacy law moves at all.

outcome.mechanism: A single House member introduced it, no one signed on, and three committees took no action on it, so it went nowhere.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 19, 2026 and referred the same day to three House committees: Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Science, Space, and Technology.
The action history shows no hearings, no markups, and no floor action after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting and selling personal data are better off, since the bill that would restrict them gained no traction in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no cosponsors have joined, so the partisan shape of support or opposition is not yet visible in the record.

industries.industry: Online advertising and ad-tech (data brokers, targeted-ad platforms)
industries.note: The bill restricts selling personal data, requires consent before profiling individuals, and bans linking ad disclosures across time to track people — the core mechanisms of behavioral advertising.

industries.industry: Large internet platforms and social media companies
industries.note: Platforms would lose their ad-profiling data practices but could still offer free services, with requirements to let users opt out of personalization; they would also face testing requirements for their consent screens and could not force users into arbitration over privacy claims.

Businesses meeting the small-business definition (under $25 million revenue, under 200 employees, not selling data) are exempt from most individual rights and minimization duties and get compliance-ramp time and shared consent templates, but all non-exempt entities must comply with the Act's core rules.

The bill requires consent before disclosing personal data to third parties and criminalizes disclosing personal information with intent to threaten or intimidate, directly targeting the resale and publication of individuals' data.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with no cosponsors and no committee action, which is the typical path for bills referred to three committees at once; without additional sponsors or a committee champion, it is likely to die at the end of the Congress. Online privacy proposals have repeatedly stalled in Congress over disagreements about a new enforcement agency, private lawsuits, and preemption of state laws, so the outlook is poor unless it gains broad bipartisan support quickly.
